knownFor: Nun of Holy Cross at Poitiers who wrote the second book of Radegund's Life, telling the coming of the relic of the Cross and Radegund's death, which Venantius Fortunatus's Life had passed over.
datesNote: No source used here gives a year of her life. Bruno Krusch dates her book soon after 600; O. M. Dalton puts it in the early years of the seventh century
placeNote: The monastery of the Holy Cross, Poitiers

keyWorks.title: Life of Radegund, Book II
keyWorks.about: written for the abbess Dedimia and the community of Holy Cross, to tell what Fortunatus passed over for length: Radegund's daily life in the monastery, the coming of the relic of the Cross, her death and burial, and miracles after it

traces: Her book is the second of the two books of Radegund's Life, after Fortunatus's, in the manuscripts Bruno Krusch edits and in Migne.
The abbess Dedimia is known only from her, Krusch notes.
An unsigned note in Migne cites her, as Fortunatus's contemporary, against scholars who struck him from the list of the bishops of Poitiers.
remembered: Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, rewrote Radegund's Life. He says he followed Fortunatus and added some miracles that Fortunatus had not touched and the nun had recorded.
Bruno Krusch judges her style very rough and says she took freely from the saints' Lives she had read; he adds that the reader will pardon good Baudonivia, who confesses her weakness.

uncertain: Her own life is thin in the sources. No source used here gives her family, her age, how she came to the house or her death, so this profile rests on her book. O. M. Dalton calls her a contemporary of Radegund who was in the monastery during Radegund's life.

Whether Radegund raised her. Her prologue says Radegund raised her from the cradle as her own household servant. Bruno Krusch notes that most of the prologue is copied from Fortunatus's prologues to his Lives of Hilary of Poitiers and Marcellus of Paris. This phrase comes from the Hilary prologue, where it is said of Pascentius, bishop of Poitiers; Krusch notes that there it means Hilary's monastery raised him, and that those who read it literally erred. So the phrase alone does not show that Radegund raised her.

The bishop in her story of the Cross. She says the bishop of the place and all the people wished to receive the relic devoutly, and the enemy of mankind worked through his agents to keep it out; she names neither the bishop nor the emperor. Gregory of Tours names the bishop, Maroveus, and says he rode off to a country estate rather than receive it; Bruno Krusch's note follows Gregory, and O. M. Dalton reads her as saying the devil seduced Maroveus and the people. Justin is Krusch's and Dalton's supplement for the emperor. The empress Sophia and the gold triptych are Dalton's words, not hers.
The year of Radegund's death. Baudonivia gives a Wednesday, the thirteenth of August, and Gregory of Tours the thirteenth day of the sixth month. The year 587 is Bruno Krusch's.
The date of her book. Soon after 600 is Krusch's reasoning, from Leifastus, a bishop of Autun she names, and from people she says are still living.

What is hers. Krusch says she copied passages from the Life of Caesarius of Arles, among them Radegund's vision of a young man a year before her death. Dalton credits her with the vision of the tribune Domolenus on the day of Radegund's death; it is in Fortunatus's Life.
Her name. One manuscript gives the book without her name, as written by one of the holy nuns who lived with Radegund.

briefReferences: Life of Radegund, Book II, prologue (ed. Bruno Krusch, MGH SRM 2, lines 29433-29440): addressed to the abbess Dedimia and the whole community, who bid her write the life of Radegund, which they know best.
Book II, prologue (MGH SRM 2, lines 29493-29496): she will tell not what Fortunatus wrote but what he passed over for length.

Book II, ch. 2 (MGH SRM 2, lines 29663-29675): told as what we heard; the shrine of the Franks burned on the queen's order, the Franks with swords and clubs, the queen unmoved on her horse until it burned.
Book II, ch. 3 (MGH SRM 2, line 29677): she left the earthly king.
Book II, ch. 5 (MGH SRM 2, lines 29743-29745): Radegund builds the monastery at Poitiers.
Book II, ch. 8 (MGH SRM 2, lines 29900-29903): Radegund's words to the community, I chose you, daughters, and the new planting.

Book II, ch. 10 (MGH SRM 2, lines 29987-29995): the same letters to each king, that they make peace and the homeland not perish; letters to their nobles; the community taught to pray and keep vigils for the kings.

Book II, ch. 16 (MGH SRM 2, lines 30238-30249): Helena and the finding of the Cross; what she did in the land of the East, blessed Radegund did in Gaul; the wood sought from the emperor, with King Sigibert's leave, for the safety of the whole homeland.
Book II, ch. 16 (MGH SRM 2, lines 30256-30262): the relic kept out of the city by the enemy of mankind through his agents, no one named.

Book II, ch. 16 (MGH SRM 2, lines 30305-30318): Radegund's fasting, vigils and tears, the community mourning and weeping every day; the king sends to Eufronius, bishop of Tours, to bring the relic into the monastery; left there for the honour of the place and the saving of the people.
Book II, ch. 21 (MGH SRM 2, lines 30516-30522): the nuns round her bed crying that their light is taken; her eyes were closed, and ours were darkened.
Book II, ch. 24 (MGH SRM 2, lines 30581-30584): the body carried under the wall, the community weeping from the wall, since no woman of the house went out of its gate.

Bruno Krusch, introduction to the Lives of Radegund (MGH SRM 2, 1888, lines 28153, 28170-28171, 28186-28193): the monastery named for the Holy Cross; Radegund's death on 13 August 587; her book written after 600, not much after.

Bruno Krusch, proemium to the prose works of Fortunatus (MGH AA 4, 1885, lines 41895-41899, 41918-41919): Radegund taken in marriage by King Chlothar I; Baudonivia's book added a little after 600; in most manuscripts Fortunatus's book and hers are joined, hers following as the second.

quotationOriginals.modern: I chose you, daughters. You are my light, my life, my rest and all my happiness. You are the new planting.
quotationOriginals.printed: Vos elegi filias, vos, raea lumina, vos, mea vita, vos, mea requies totaque felici- > 'tas, vos, novella plantatio.
quotationOriginals.work: Baudonivia, Life of Radegund, Book II, ch. 8, ed. Bruno Krusch
quotationOriginals.uncertain: In the Latin, filias is not an address: Radegund says she chose them as daughters, and the brief renders it as I chose you, daughters. The scan prints raea for mea.
